I am a social scientist interested in how and why people believe or like certain evidence or information. I use various methods including experiments, cross-sectional surveys, and panel surveys in my research. I am also trained in more advanced quantitative methods, such as SEM, social network analysis, and psychometrics. My work has received two top paper panel awards at the National Communication Association Conference (Social Cognition Division in 2025, Political Communication Division in 2025).

Dissertation
{{</color>}}
{{</centered>}}
{{</poet>}}
{{</text-font>}}

My dissertation examines when, why, and for whom narrative evidence may be more persuasive than factual evidence. Drawing on dual-process theories, narrative persuasion, processing fluency, and epistemology, this work develops a theoretically grounded account of how audiences evaluate competing forms of evidence. More broadly, the dissertation serves as the foundation of my long-term research agenda on communicating evidence across political, ideological, and epistemic divides. By identifying the conditions under which different forms of evidence are persuasive, this research has the potential to advance both communication theory and evidence-based communication practice.
